titleFa: کتاب The Unbearable Lightness of Being
author: Milan Kundera
introFa: کتاب «The Unbearable Lightness of Being» نوشته Milan Kundera یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The Unbearable Lightness of Being»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 23 Film Matters Fall 2013 ➜ WITHIN POPULAR DISCOURSE ON film adaption, the “unfilmable” novel is a prevalent designation. It suggests that literary works of pronounced singularity defy filmic translation, as if its demands exceed the representational abilities of cinema. Time and time again, however, filmmakers have taken on seemingly impossible and complex plotlines and turned them into coherent films. From James Joyce’s Ulysses (1922) to William S. Burroughs’ Naked Lunch (1959), many of the twentieth century’s most difficult novels have found their way to the screen. Among such films is Philip Kaufman’s 1988 adaptation of Milan Kundera’s highly idiosyncratic novel The Unbearable Lightness of Being: A Novel (1984), providing itself as a fascinating case study in adaptation studies. It represents an attempt to narrativize a formally hybrid text, wherein an unknown narrator prefaces chapters of dramatic action with essayistic meditations on such various matters as love, linguistics, Czech identity, and philosophy. These interpolations provide a unificatory function in that they contextualize the actions of its characters within the scope of Kundera’s thesis. Interestingly, despite its importance, Kaufman eliminates the unknown narrator from the film. This is a curious adaptive decision, one that warrants our attention. What then becomes of the contextual coherence of the dramatic action? It is this The “Unfilmable” Lightness of Being?: Essayistic Devices in Kaufman’s Adaptation of The Unbearable Lightness of Being By Brandon Konecny keywords: adaptation studies, essay film, narratology, Philip Kaufman, Milan Kundera, The Unbearable Lightness of Being, literature Feature 04 figure 2

24 Film Matters Fall 2013 Feature 04 question that is of particular interest here. Two objectives thus occupy the terrain of this essay: (1) to elucidate the tenets of the essayistic form, particularly as it relates to cinema, and (2) show how its constitutive devices can enable the adaptation of a hybrid text within the confines of popular narrative cinema. The former requires engaging with the essay film and defining its objectives and formal constituents. Moreover, it demands brief historical consideration of the long-held assumption that, as David Bordwell writes, “fictional narrative [is] the prototype for all cinema” (13). Doing so, in toto, will illustrate that the essay film enables a highly personal mode of filmmaking, wherein the use of self-reflexivity, expressive performances, and found footage allows filmmakers to maneuver between the polarities of fiction and nonfiction. It transgresses the conception of cinema as strictly storytelling medium and subordinates narrative to the demonstration of the author’s thesis. For the latter, I turn my attention to Kaufman’s adaptation of Kundera’s novel, specifically focusing on the film’s elimination the novel’s narrator and its ramifications on the contextual coherence of the dramatic action. Kaufman reconciles this absence, I claim, by way of his use of the three aforesaid essayistic devices, serving as cinematic substitutes for Kundera’s essayistic asides. Ultimately, it is my intent to show that Kaufman’s adaptive use of the essayistic mode allows for the flow of narrative apropos of exoteric cinema while giving Kundera’s thesis regarding the experiential dimensions of human existence legible presence. Probing the Essayistic In regards to the essayistic form, it occupies a liminal area of artistic expression. Its modal hybridity makes the delineation between fiction and nonfiction nebulous, if not irrelevant, and such liminality has in turn left defining the form difficult. Laura Rascaroli, attesting to this notion, writes that “although widely used, the category is under-theorized, more so than other forms” (21). In an attempt to elaborate her own conception of the mode, she sites common devices that are indicative of the essayistic, including self-reflexivity, authorial presence, and the subordination of the chronotope – that is, the time and space of the diegesis – and performers to the author’s thesis. These details, while enlightening, are nonetheless sparse, leaving the specificities of the essayistic form to remain debatable. It is telling about the mode’s formal idiosyncrasies but not of its objectives. However, since a definitive example is necessary here, specifically to justify Kundera’s work as essayistic, let us reference Aldous Huxley’s quite thorough account of the essay. He purports that the essay moves among three poles: (1) the personal and autobiographical; (2) the objective, the factual, the concrete-particular; and (3) the abstract universal. Furthermore, he propounds that, although the achievement of only one of these elements is sufficient for the designation of an essay, “the most richly satisfying essays are those which make the best not of one, but not of two, but all three worlds in which it is possible for the essay to exist” (Corrigan 14). With consideration to its first-person narration, metahistoricity, and dense philosophical asides, Kundera’s novel is in exact accordance with Huxley’s qualification of a richly satisfying essay. However, it is precisely the novel’s essayistic classification that renders it problematic in the realm of film adaptation, since cinema has historically favored a quite rigid delineation between fiction and nonfiction. Cinema, Narrativity, and the Essay Film’s Modal Trangressions Writing on the ontology of cinema, Alain Badiou argues, “film would not exist, or would not have existed, without the novel” (89). His statement harbors the assumption that there is an inherent novelistic conditioning in film, like a compulsory drive embedded within the medium itself, continually pushing it to inhabit the domain of narrativity. The history of cinema, by and large, supports Badiou’s assertion. From its earliest years, the medium has largely been devoted to the development of a film language subservient to fictional narrative. This has resulted, as Christian Metz writes, in “all nonnarrative genres… [becoming] marginal provinces, border regions so to speak, while the feature-length film of novelistic fiction, which is simply called ‘film’… has traced more and more clearly the king’s highway of filmic expression” (Metz’s emphasis, 94). That is, the cinematic modal hierarchy, with narrative cinema as its hierarch, relegates nonnarative modes – experimental, documentary, industrial, etc. – to peripheral existences, and thereby preserves the formal distinction between fiction and nonfiction. The fictional narrative film is, therefore, assumed to be the essence of cinema, to be its prototype. Avant-garde and art cinema, in contrast, have long since jettisoned these strict demarcations, frequently producing works that exhibit an intersection of fiction and nonfiction, formulating of a hybrid film language in which subjectivity and objectivity Brandon Konecny In this sense, it is just as much Kundera as Tereza silently looking down at the dead Czech bodies. figure 1 figure 3

25 Film Matters Fall 2013 ➜ experienced it, and that the recurrence itself recurs ad infinitum… …[T]he idea of eternal return implies a perspective from which things appear other than as we know them: they appear without the mitigating circumstances of their transitory nature. This mitigating circumstance prevents us from coming to a verdict. (Kundera 3–4) The eternal return, in other words, suggests that every moment of one’s life, in all its perceived uniquity, is illusory, merely a recapitulation of moments prior. And it is because of one’s innate limited perspective, the stringent binding of their field of awareness to the accessible present, that every moment is understood to be ephemeral, thus escaping their informed judgment. One cannot fully, in a word, conceive of their experiences within the totality of their existence, for doing so would transgress their ontology, what it means to be human. To legibly insert such a complex, metaphysical notion into narrative cinema is an arduous undertaking, to say the least – especially with the deletion of Kundera’s narration, who explicitly details the intricacies of this philosophy throughout the text. The absence of the narrator aside, much of this difficulty, I claim, is to be located in the representational logic of cinema itself, a medium that is wedded to literal phenomenality. The novel is not constrained by this necessity, however. For the freedom of prose, as Badiou points modes of representation in order to alter the signifying work of the cinema and thereby engage the audience at different levels” (López 142). Alea’s film, in short, shows the essayistic to be highly rhetorical and personally expressive mode of filmmaking. Demonstration of such a film language in the realm of popular cinema is unfortunately scarce. This paucity reveals Kaufman’s film to an exemplary case of the convergence of the essayistic and narrativity in popular cinema. Having established the tenets of the essayistic mode, let us turn to Kaufman’s film and explore the ways in which he employs the same triad of essayistic devices within the context of popular cinema to attempt to translate the dictates of Kundera’s idiosyncratic, hybrid novel. Self-Reflexivity and Nietzsche’s “Eternal Return” Kaufman makes great use of self-reflexivity to give presence to Kundera’s philosophical inquiry of Friedrich Nietzsche’s “eternal return.” This adaptive decision is noteworthy for us, for it shows a clever use of the cinema qua visual medium. He, as Annette Insdorf posits, “invokes the eternal return in a cinematic manner, the image repeating itself ” (Insdorf 17). This notion is cardinal in the contextualization of the Kundera’s narrative. According to him, the notion of the eternal return: …is a mysterious one, and Nietzsche has often perplexed other philosophers with it: to think that everything recurs as we once coalesce to assume a critical dimension. Filmmakers such as Tomás Gutiérrez Alea, Dušan Makavejev, Chris Marker, Jean- Luc Godard, Jonas Mekas, and Werner Hertzog have greatly advanced the filmic junction of subjectivity and objectivity, and they have frequently been referred to in academic discourse as essayistic filmmakers. For demonstrative purposes, let us briefly examine an essay film, namely, Tomás Gutiérrez Alea’s Memories of Underdevelopment (1968), a character study of Sergio and his alienation amid the tumult of social changes in post-revolutionary Cuba. To explore the implications of the recent political activity, Alea exemplarily uses the above-mentioned triad of devices. First, he utilizes various self-reflexive devices redolent of European art cinema – freeze frames, photographs, etc. – to disrupt the normal passivity of spectatorship, which enables viewers to comprehend that the content on the screen possesses a pointed rhetorical function, whose relevance extends beyond the duration of the film. As for expressive performances, Sergio exhibits and perceives elements of post-revolutionary Cuba that are situated in such a way as to appear problematic for advancement. He is, as an example, the embodiment of Latin machismo, exposed in all its vulgarity. Further, Elena, his once girlfriend, and her family attempt to sue him for “taking advantage of her,” lying in court and claiming that she is mentally handicapped, hence justifying her out-of-wedlock relations. This shows the lingering gender inequality and conservatism of the country. Finally, the film interpolates newsreel footage and photographs of recent historical events. In one case, when Sergio and his friend discuss the Bay of Pigs, the film cuts to footage of the prisoners, each of them being marched forward at gunpoint, their hands above their heads (see Figure 1). The film, via its usage of these essayistic devices, consistently “complicates the protocols necessary for their reception, mixing documentary and fictional Feature 04 The “Unfilmable” Lightness of Being?: Essayistic Devices in Kaufman’s Adaptation… …it is because of one’s innate limited perspective, the stringent binding of one’s fi eld of awareness to accessible present, that every moment is understood to be ephemeral, thus escaping one’s informed judgment. figure 4 figure 5

26 Film Matters Fall 2013 This formal device, contra the paradigms of popular cinema, disrupts the immersive nature of spectatorship in a phenomenological manner, giving awareness to, in Hegel’s parlance, the viewer’s “sense- certainly”: the viewer is now, as it were, presented with a reflection of reality rather than reality itself – and the difference is negligible. This reflection renders the profilmic action so precisely, so seamlessly, that if the scene were to have begun just at the moment of the frame’s enclosure of mirror’s reflection, the spectator would be unaware of its reflective origin. It would be an unnoticeable replacement of the real, which reminds one of the limits of our own perception (see Figure 4). This new angle, moreover, reveals the presence of two other mirrors placed in the mise-en-scéne, each of which reproduces the motions of the lovemaking from various angles. It is as if the characters’ consumption of the moment, in its perceived ephemerality, stultifies their cognition that their copulation is but a reflection of the past. The multiple reflections thus appropriately bespeak Kundera’s description of the eternal return: our experiences are recurrences of prior moments; however, the limits of human perception do not allow for conscious recognition of the experiential familiarity. Expressive Performances and the Weight of Existence In addition to his use of reflexivity, Kaufman utilizes expressive performances whereby the denotative actions of the dramatis personae – that is, the primary signification of their actions within the diegesis – have another layer, a secondary signification, which connotatively attest to the author’s thesis. Characters are hence rhetorical tools. This adaptive strategy is fitting for the adaptation of Kundera’s novel wherein his “meditative interpolations” transform the characters’ actions into illustration of his thesis (Kundera The Curtain 69). In the novel, for instance, Kundera classifies the characters’ actions in The mirror is, at a physical level, inherently indicative of the eternal return. If one stands in front of a mirror, light rays reflect off their body and stream toward the mirror in a linear trajectory. These rays of light, or “photons,” shoot through the glass, hitting the silver coating. They are reflected off this surface and continue to travel in the given space. The individual perceives the organization of these light rays as a reflection of themselves. Moreover, as light rays are reflected from the mirror, they again reflect off the surface of the individual’s body, which direct the photons back toward the mirror. This process, insofar as one remains in front of the mirror, is repeated ad infinitum (Giancoli 838–39). The point here is that the physical properties of the mirror, with its constant direction of photons, makes it an appropriate object to symbolize the eternal return. The scene in which three mirrors, each situated in various locations in the profilmic space encompassing Tomas’ and Sabina’s copulation, offers itself as a precise demonstration of Kaufman’s cinematic translation of this Nietzschean notion. It commences with a medium shot of Tomas and Sabina having sex. As Sabina presses Tomas’ body flat on the bed, the camera gradually follows their movement, tilting down while simultaneously panning right, revealing a large mirror situated in front of the bed (see Figure 2). The camera booms slightly upwards and begins to zoom in toward the mirror, which now reflects their lovemaking from a straight-on angle. It ceases to zoom when their reflection in the mirror consumes the entirety of the frame (see Figure 3). out, “lies in not having to put bodies on display,” i.e., that it does not have to give entities visible literality (89). This is particularly problematic to translate a narrator who is so present in the novel, yet is never declaratively introduced as a specific character. Despite the elimination of the knowledgeable narrator, this philosophical notion is not wholly absent. It is not communicated to the viewer via “the word”—expologue, voiceover, titlecards, etc. Kaufman, rather than attempt to overtly translate Kundera’s labyrinthine explanation of the eternal return, which spans nearly four pages, utilizes the essayistic device of self-reflexivity to render it in a symbolic manner. Specifically, Kaufman invokes Nietzsche’s eternal return through the reflexive device of mise en abyme, whereby one’s image is reflected amongst multiple mirrors. Throughout the film, for example, Kaufman situates multiple mirrors within the mise-en-scéne. In consequence, the excessive multiplication of the characters’ images within the profilmic space makes the viewer aware of their own spectatorship, removing their passivity and enabling them to critically evaluate the images. Thus, although Kaufman does not overtly reference Nietzsche’s eternal return, his use of mise en abyme allows the viewer to extrapolate that the infinite reflection of images possess some narrative significance, something of which they should be aware. However, before I explicate how Kaufman demonstrates this reflexivity in the film, I want us to look at why the usage of mirrors is a fitting means to connote the eternal return. 27 Film Matters Fall 2013 ➜ relation to Parmenides’ division of lightness and weight: [Parmenides] saw the world divided into pairs of opposites…[For example] lightness is positive, weight negative. Was he correct or not? That is the question. The only certainty is: the lightness/weight opposition is the most mysterious, most ambiguous of all (Kundera 5–6). He thus, taxonomically, observes the characters’ behavior as either connotatively “light” or “heavy.” In the case of Tomas, he initially lives a life of lightness, enjoying his revered social status, promiscuity, etc. In commencing with his relationship with Tereza, though, he increasingly assumes a life of heaviness, now “burdened” with the responsibilities of another’s happiness. Tereza, in contrast, begins with a heavy existence. She lives in an isolated village and works a demanding working-class job. But throughout her relationship with Tomas, she attains lightness, coming to terms with many of her internal struggles. Hence, it is Tomas and Tereza’s relationship that catalyzes their existential shifts; and the novel concludes with their attainment of equilibrium, whereby they both achieve a homeostatic lightness together prior to their tragic, albeit eluded, deaths. But how does one cinematically show this initial shift? With the absence of the narrator, Kaufman contextualizes these existential progressions through expressive, rhetorically informed performances. A good example of this is the scene where Tomas awakes next to Tereza after their first night together. The scene begins with a shot of an alarm clock on a shelf. As it begins to ring, Tomas’ hand enters from the bottom of the frame and clumsily turns it off. The camera moves in motion with Tomas’ arms as he slowly retracts it to his body, panning downwards to a medium close-up of him lying in bed. His seemingly lone presence in his bed, an assumption resulting from the constrained visibility of Kaufman’s framing, connotes the “lightness” of his lifestyle, free from any responsibility (see Figure 5). However, as he slowly attempts to arise out of bed, he is stopped. The camera quickly pans toward the right, revealing Tereza’s hand as it tightly grips his. He turns to look toward her, the camera following his gaze, and the film shows her lying beside him, her disheveled hair and rosy cheeks giving her visage an innocent, childlike quality. Tomas turns his attention back to their clasped hands, which the camera shows in close-up, as if to punctuate the image’s symbolic weight. He attempts to free his hand from her grip, but their fingers remain tightly intertwined. In a second attempt, Tomas retrieves Sophocles’ Oedipus Rex from his nightstand and brings the book toward their grasp and furtively works it into her hand (see Figure 6), freeing himself from the weight of being bound to a woman by way of artifice. Immediately after, Kaufman makes his first cut in the scene, showing a medium close-up of Tomas kissing Tereza’s hand as it grasps Sophocles’ canonical tragedy. His actions suggest that, despite being freed of her grasp, he has acquired an emotional connection to her, a connotative weight. He leaves the bed, and the film cuts to a high-angle shot of Tereza holding the book as the camera slowly zooms in to a medium close-up of her face (see Figure 7). Her lone presence in the bed, in contrast, connotes the acquirement of lightness, which Kaufman punctuates with the high-angle zoom. The Revisitation of Trauma through Found Footage In addition to his use of expressive performances, Kaufman employs found footage to translate Kundera’s description of the 1968 Russian invasion of Czechoslovakia in an emotionally charged manner and allow for authorial comment at a critical distance. Describing the historical event in the novel, Kundera writes, “Czech photographers and cameramen were acutely aware that they were the ones who could best do the only thing left to do: preserve the face of violence for the distant future” (Kundera 67). Kundera’s description is a personal revisitation of the historical event, as if to, in a psychoanalytic sense, return to an original site (or sight) of trauma. It is both descriptive in its historical exposition and highly reflective. To translate the novel’s metahistoricity, Kaufman decides to embed the viewer within this traumatic revisitation, using newsreel footage of the event and seamlessly intercutting it with fictional footage of Tomas and Tereza. Kaufman, furthermore, films the fictional footage with old newsreel film stock and purposely scratches and desaturates it to give the images textural uniformity (Insdorf 27). This precisely exemplifies the hybridity of the essayistic, the convergence of the fictive and nonfictive, but it also enables the main characters to become expressive entities for Kundera’s authorial comment on the historical event. 28 Film Matters Fall 2013 having done what was necessary, exits the frame with Tomas following closely behind her. Hence, these characters, which are, as we established, demonstrative entities for his thesis, are the bearers of Kundera’s trauma. By cutting between footage of these characters in their fictional context and actual footage of the invasion, Kaufman, I argue, allows an engagement with past trauma, a means by which to evaluate it from a critical dimension, while still preserving the pain of the past. In this sense, it is just as much Kundera as Tereza silently looking down at the dead Czech bodies. Conclusion Reflection on Kaufman’s film proves to be an illuminative endeavor. In adapting Kundera’s hybrid text, his clever use of formal devices normally germane to the essay film enables much of the novel’s philosophical concerns to be perceptible on-screen. Via self- reflexivity, expressive performances, and found footage, the philosophical dimensions of the novel such as Nietzsche’s eternal return, Parmenides’ binaristic taxonomy of the world, and its metahistorical criticism have a pronounced presence in the narrative. And these essayistic devices, be they utilized consciously or symptomatically in response to the novel’s demands, fittingly preserves the contextual legibility of the dramatic action, allowing concepts to be rendered in a symbolic fashion. In the end, The Unbearable Lightness of Being demonstrates that the implementation of cinematic language outside of the lexicon of narrative film can forge new paths for popular cinema, as well as film adaptation, expanding the realm of its possibilities. Kaufman’s innovation in this film shows the remarkable ability of cinema to translate what is on the page with the specificities of its own medium – framing, staging, editing, etc. – and thereby continually challenge the concept of the “unfilmable” novel. /end/ It must be said, however, that authorial comment, stricto sensu, would require the presence of Kundera himself behind the camera, not Kaufman. This begs the question of, how can Kaufman’s use of found footage, in accordance to the tenets of the essayistic form, truly allow authorial comment? In the realm of adaption, these stringent definitions are malleable, I claim, especially in the context of studio productions wherein numerous individuals contribute to a single product. Kaufman’s direction, mutatis mutandis, attains a surrogate first-person function, whereby “the ‘I’ of Kundera’s text [is replaced] with the ‘eye’ [of] cinematic storytelling” (Insdorf 28). The first-person narration, in other words, is transmuted to the eye of Kaufman’s camera, rendering the duty of the camera to the interpreter of the novel’s narration. The film’s characters, then, are Kundera’s proxies for authorial commentary on Russia’s 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia. A good example of this metahistorical criticism is Tereza’s first photographs of dead citizens during the invasion. In the scene, newsreel footage shows Czech citizens carrying a dead man’s body away from the frantic crowd in the streets. The film cuts to a group of people standing solemnly in an alleyway, among which are Tomas and Tereza, all of them collectively gazing downwards at two dead bodies. Cutting back to newsreel footage of the event, Kaufman shows two men as they cover one of the bodies with the Czechoslovakian flag (see Figure 8). It cuts to a close-up of Tereza’s face as she morosely fixates on the dead bodies, her physiognomy communicating a sense of helplessness and despair (see Figure 9). In a decisive moment, she jettisons her reticence and begins to reach for her camera. The camera moves in motion with her as she kneels on the ground and, recalling Kaufman’s description, begins doing “the only thing left to do” – take photographs. Kaufman cuts back to the actual found footage of the two bloody bodies lying on the ground. He cuts back to an establishing shot of the alleyway as she takes her last few photographs. 29 Film Matters Fall 2013 ➜ Author Biography Brandon Konecny recently graduated from the Film Studies program at the University of North Carolina Wilmington. He is a two-time scholarship recipient of the Fluor Scholarship Foundation, winner of the UNCW Award for Excellence in Film Studies, and recently completed his honors thesis Images of Marginality: The Representation of Youth Subcultures in American Cinema, 1953–1994. He has also presented at the Visions Film Festival and Conference wherein he received the excellence in scholarship award. He is currently an “In the Field” writer for Film International, and frequently researches such topics as post-war American avant-garde film, Eastern European cinema, Žižekian film theory, Cinema Novo, Christopher Maclaine, fandom studies, and Cold War era science fiction. His work has appeared in the Monroe Enquirer Journal, Film International, Journal of Religion & Film, and Intellect’s Journal of Fandom Studies (forthcoming). He soon plans to attend law school and pursue a career in transactional entertainment law. Mentor Biography Mariana Johnson, Professor of Film Studies at the University of North Carolina Wilmington, teaches courses in Latin American cinema, world cinema, and the history of documentary. She received her PhD in Cinema Studies from New York University, where she also earned a graduate certificate in ethnographic filmmaking from the Program for Media, Culture and History. A Film Society of Lincoln Center Fellowship recipient, she has been published in Film Comment, The Oxford American, Film International, Television and New Media, and Studies in Hispanic Cinemas. Her book chapters have appeared in the Oxford Handbook of Film and Media Studies (Oxford University Press) and Contemporary Spanish Cinema and Genre (Manchester University Press). She is currently editing the Directory of World Cinema: Cuba (Intellect Press) and working on a project about film preservation in Latin America. Department Overview The Film Studies major at UNCW develops students’ analytical, research, and writing skills, as well as their creative and technical abilities.
